lines.text: Without rain, the Panama Canal stops.
So what if it never rained there again?
It nearly happened. In a drought, the canal cut the ships crossing each day from 36 to just 22.
Why would a canal need rain? It isn't a flat ditch from sea to sea. Ships climb up into a lake in the middle of Panama, Gatun Lake, then step back down to the other ocean.
And where does the water go? Every ship that crosses lets a huge gulp of the lake's fresh water run out into the sea.
The only thing that fills it back up is rain, falling on the forest all around it.
So if the rain stops for good, the lake sinks a little with every ship, the locks run short, and fewer and fewer ships get through.
At both ends, the line of waiting ships grows longer every day, each one loaded with cargo that someone, somewhere, is waiting for.

Until the only way left is the long way round: all the way down South America, round stormy Cape Horn, and back up the other side. Weeks at sea, instead of about half a day going straight through the canal.
And about 5% of all the world's trade by sea goes through this one canal: cars, grain and fuel. All of it riding on the rain.
Rain or ships: which does Panama need more? Tell me. Because without rain,
